summary: Specifies a standard method of encapsulating IP datagrams on NetBIOS networks, so IP traffic can travel over such networks.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1088 says how to send Internet Protocol (IP) messages over a NetBIOS network. It matters because programs written for IP can run on that kind of network with no address lookup service.

questions: encapsulate ip datagrams on netbios networks
how are netbios names built from ip addresses
what is the mtu for ip over netbios
how does ip run over netbios
subtitle: How to carry IP datagrams inside NetBIOS datagrams by building each NetBIOS name from an IP address.

tldr.problem: Programs on a NetBIOS network want to use IP, but there was no agreed way to put IP datagrams into NetBIOS datagrams.
tldr.mechanism: Each IP datagram is sent as the data of one NetBIOS datagram, and each host's NetBIOS name is built from its IP address, so no address lookup is needed.
tldr.outcome: It is an Internet Standard. Broadcast uses one special group name, multicast is not supported, and the maximum packet size is 512 bytes.

today: RFC 1088 is an Internet Standard, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 1088 sets one standard way to encapsulate Internet Protocol (RFC 791) datagrams inside NetBIOS datagrams, so that separate implementations can interoperate. NetBIOS can also create virtual circuits and send point-to-point, multicast and broadcast datagrams, but this specification uses only its datagram services.

Hosts on a NetBIOS network are given IP numbers, so IP-based applications work there. A router that can also encapsulate IP packets in ordinary data-link protocols such as 802.3 lets those hosts reach the wider Internet. The RFC notes that earlier versions of the memo used the NetBIOS broadcast datagram service for IP broadcasting instead of group names, and that those versions are now obsolete.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC defines one shared way to put Internet packets into NetBIOS envelopes, so that equipment from different makers works together.

sections.title: Names Built from IP Addresses
sections.content:
A NetBIOS name may be any series of 16 bytes, though a few values are reserved by common networking packages. For IP applications the name is chosen from the host's internet number: IP.XX.XX.XX.XX is the NetBIOS name of any IP over NetBIOS host, where each XX is the ASCII hexadecimal representation of that byte of the internet address.

Because NetBIOS names are a mapping of IP addresses, no physical address query mechanism such as ARP is required. The addressing scheme also allows standard datagram protocols to be multiplexed over NetBIOS and lets a person confirm by eye that a packet's address is correct.
sections.plainLanguage: Each computer's network name is made directly from its IP address, so nothing has to look the name up before sending.

sections.title: Broadcast, Multicast and MTU
sections.content:
Broadcast internet addresses are represented by the NetBIOS group name IP.FF.FF.FF.FF. At present no attempt is made to support IP multicast addresses using NetBIOS group names.

The maximum data size of a NetBIOS datagram is 512 bytes, and therefore the Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU) for IP over NetBIOS networks is 512 bytes. Hosts communicating with a host on a NetBIOS network may therefore be required to reassemble fragmented datagrams.
sections.plainLanguage: Messages to everyone go to one shared name. Each envelope holds at most 512 bytes, so larger packets are split into pieces and put back together.

sections.title: Starting and Stopping IP Support
sections.content:
To support IP for a given address, the initialization code must add IP.XX.XX.XX.XX to the host's NetBIOS name table, add IP.FF.FF.FF.FF to the host's group name table, and submit a receive datagram request for each of the two names. When a datagram arrives it is processed by the protocol stack and another receive request is submitted.

Sending an IP datagram means treating it as NetBIOS datagram data and using a send datagram request to IP.XX.XX.XX.XX or IP.FF.FF.FF.FF. Adapter status queries are optional, though the RFC says they may become mandatory as SNMP support becomes a requirement for IP hosts. When IP support is discontinued, a cancel request is submitted for every pending receive and a delete name request for both names.
sections.plainLanguage: A host registers its two names at start-up and listens for messages on them, and it removes them when it stops speaking IP.
